And on the topic of the ramifications of this case…

We can expect to see a lot of these retaliatory lawsuits against #MeToo survivors. This is a nightmare.

The #MeToo moment lost momentum before we made any structural changes to how we treat survivors. Our legal system is still the same one that betrays victims over and over again.

Remember that as these #MeToo men get acquitted or win civil lawsuits. They're still at an advantage.

It's one of the reasons the benefits of the #MeToo Movement haven't necessarily extended to women of color or poverty- or working-class women. The media version of the movement really centered white wealthy women's experiences.

“What do we need to do to prevent anyone else from having to say #MeToo?”

https://t.co/955DYM17ZR

In the first phase of the #MeToo Movement, we raised awareness about gender-based violence and empathy for survivors.

In the second phase, let us change the very fiber for our society to ensure—for the first time ever—that women can live a life without violence.

This verdict is not a surprise—and it doesn’t signal the death of #MeToo.

It’s a reminder of why we need #MeToo in the first place.

For feminists, this should be a radicalizing moment, inspiring us to push for structural changes to the systems stacked against us.

What are the biggest takeaways from Depp v. Heard? I shared my thoughts in Time about what the verdict teaches us about #MeToo (and the need for structural change).

https://t.co/7qnLWldx0f

@wagatwe @MoiraDonegan @lesbrains The mainstream framing of the #MeToo movement really erased gender from the discussion. It was all about men abusing their power over women at work. And so it isn’t surprising that many people would see removing women from the workplace as the solution.
I just can’t bring myself to read another op-ed about how the fall of Roe v. Wade or the backlash to the #MeToo movement is the fault of feminists.
